question: A 14-year-old boy has a BMI of 27 kg/m². His mother states that her own BMI is 29 and asks whether her son is 'obese like me'. Which statement is most accurate regarding obesity classification in adolescents?

answers.text: A BMI of 27 kg/m² is in the overweight/obese adult range; the same cut-offs apply to this 14-year-old.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Adult BMI cut-offs (overweight ≥25, obese ≥30) do NOT apply to children and adolescents because body composition changes markedly with age and sex. Paediatric classification requires age- and sex-adjusted BMI-for-age percentile charts.

answers.text: Adolescent obesity requires BMI-for-age interpretation using age- and sex-adjusted reference standards (IAP/WHO charts); an absolute BMI of 27 cannot be directly interpreted without chart plotting.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In children and adolescents, obesity is classified using BMI-for-age on IAP 2015 (for Indian children 5–18 yr) or WHO charts — not fixed adult cut-offs. The 14-year-old's BMI must be plotted to determine his BMI-for-age percentile (overweight ≥85th, obese ≥95th on IAP charts).

answers.text: Obesity in adolescents is diagnosed clinically by inspection alone; BMI measurement is not necessary in this age group.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. BMI-for-age is the standard diagnostic tool for adolescent obesity. Clinical inspection underestimates central/metabolic obesity and is not a substitute for measurement.

answers.text: The IOTF cut-offs (international reference) are mandatory for classifying obesity in all Indian adolescents.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The IAP 2015 reference charts are the recommended standard for Indian children aged 5–18 years. IOTF cut-offs are used for international comparisons and research but are not the primary clinical reference in India.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key principle: adolescent obesity classification uses BMI-for-age on IAP/WHO reference charts, not the adult BMI cut-offs. Plot the value, then interpret the percentile.
Correct. Adolescent BMI must be interpreted using age- and sex-adjusted BMI-for-age charts (IAP 2015 for Indian children). Adult BMI cut-offs do not apply.
